idiom_name: extension (m: Movable) def moveTo(...) - resolved like a member call
implementation_notes: Scala 3 makes the servant a language construct: extension methods add behaviour to a type after it is defined, are found through the receiver's implicit scope or an import, and are rewritten by the compiler into a call with the receiver as the first argument. The capability is expressed as the receiver type or a context bound (extension [T: Movable](t: T)), so the serviced classes declare nothing extra. For behaviour that must vary per serviced type, the Scala type-class form - a capability trait with given instances plus a servant function def render[T: Show](t: T) - is the other standard realization and is often preferred when the capabilities multiply. A plain servant object stays justified when the behaviour carries mutable policy or must be injected for tests, since neither extension methods nor given instances can be substituted per call.
pitfalls: Extension methods are resolved statically and never override: an existing member of the same name wins, and an extension that is not imported is invisible - the compiler explains it with 'value moveTo is not a member of ...; could be made available as an extension method'.
Two eligible extensions (one from the receiver's implicit scope, one from a given instance) make the selection ambiguous: keep servant extensions in one object per service and import them explicitly.
sources: Scala documentation, Extension Methods (Scala 3 reference) - definition, translation and the four ways an extension becomes applicable; https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/contextual/extension-methods.html
Scala documentation, Extension Methods (Scala 3 book) - notes that Scala 2 achieved the same with implicit classes; https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/book/ca-extension-methods.html

variants.name: Scala 2 implicit class wrapper
variants.idiom_name: implicit class MoveOps(m: Movable) extends AnyVal
variants.implementation_notes: In Scala 2 the servant is an implicit class wrapping the serviced value: the declaration is placed in an object, the call site imports it, and the compiler inserts the wrapper conversion so the method reads as a member (the 'pimp my library' idiom). Extending AnyVal keeps the wrapper allocation-free; without it every call boxes a new wrapper, which is exactly the overhead that Scala 3 extension methods remove. The capability interface is the wrapper's parameter type, and the same object can group several servants over different capabilities - this remains the only option on Scala 2.13 codebases.
pitfalls: Because the mechanism is an implicit conversion, the wrapper applies wherever the import is visible - values of the wrapped type silently gain the methods, and a mistaken import changes which overload is chosen.
Forgetting extends AnyVal allocates a wrapper per call, and implicit classes can never be top-level declarations: they must live inside an object, class or trait and be imported per call site.
sources: Scala documentation, Relationship with Scala 2 Implicits - extension methods have no direct Scala 2 counterpart but can be simulated with implicit classes; https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/contextual/relationship-implicits.html
Scala documentation, Scala 3 Reference index - 'extension methods replace implicit classes with a clearer and simpler mechanism'; https://docs.scala-lang.org/scala3/reference/index.html
